newsitem.title: USA: Electronic Atlas weds rainfall, climate worldwide.
newsitem.headline: Electronic Atlas weds rainfall, climate worldwide.

text.p: Scientists have created an electronic Atlas that needs only seconds to show rainfall and climate data for any neighbourhood, region, country or continent -- potentially a tool for anyone interested in crops or water supplies.
"I have no idea what all the applications will be," Donald Jensen, one of the developers, said in an interview last week. "It really does put all the data ... in one place."

David Seckler, head of the International Irrigation Management Institute (IIMI) in Colombo, Sri Lanka, said the Atlas provided an easy way to match crops to regions with favourable climates. Otherwise, farmers would have to learn by trial and error if a crop would thrive.
"This helps define the agro-economic zone," said Seckler, who called the Atlas "a big incremental step" in making a vast array of data easily accessible and useful for agriculture.
The World Water and Climate Atlas for Agriculture was developed by IIMI and Jensen's Utah Climate Centre at Utah State University, Logan, Utah, with funding from the government of Japan.

It will be available by CD-ROM and on the Internet. The first CD, dealing with Asia, was released on Friday. CDs covering the rest of the world will be available by year's end. The entire Atlas would be available over the Internet in July, developers said (http://atlas.usu.edu). At present, only the Asia section is available.

Information can be summoned for areas as small as one square mile (2.5 sq km). Data on small areas could be useful for planning irrigation projects or deciding how large a reservoir should be, Jensen said. For larger areas, the information also can be displayed on colour-coded maps.

In a demonstration for reporters, Jensen used a year-long sequence of maps to show monsoons beating their way northward across India. As rainfall spread, ever-larger sections of India turned a deep blue, the colour denoting heavy rains.

Data from 56,000 weather stations worldwide was used in compiling the Atlas, which is based on weather from 1961-90. The Atlas includes 10-day, monthly and annual summaries of average, maximum and minimum temperatures, precipitation, precipitation probabilities and evapotranspiration, the amount of water evaporated from bodies of water and growing crops.
It also has two indices, one showing if there is enough moisture in a region for crops and the other showing areas that would need irrigation to supplement rainfall.
Seckler said the Atlas would become more valuable in coming years as competition for water becomes stronger. Agriculture accounts for 70 percent of water use.
